PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Nullifies state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Fiscal Impact: The net fiscal effect is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. Supporters: CA Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association (CalTax) Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Californians deserve better results for our taxes. Billions have flowed into programs like homelessness, with too little to show for it. Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct PUBLIC AUDITS of programs funded by new taxes—so we get more transparency, more accountability and better outcomes for taxpayers.
CON
Prop. 41 isn’t really about audits—it’s a billionaire-funded trick designed to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Vote NO on 41.

PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Nullifies state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Fiscal Impact: The net fiscal effect is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. Supporters: CA Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association (CalTax) Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Californians deserve better results for our taxes. Billions have flowed into programs like homelessness, with too little to show for it. Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct PUBLIC AUDITS of programs funded by new taxes—so we get more transparency, more accountability and better outcomes for taxpayers.
CON
Prop. 41 isn’t really about audits—it’s a billionaire-funded trick designed to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Vote NO on 41.

This proposition would make it harder to pass new special taxes by requiring the state auditor to review any special tax proposal before it goes to voters.

This proposition would make it harder to pass new special taxes by requiring the state auditor to review any special tax proposal before it goes to voters.

If this proposition receives more votes than Proposition 40 (a wealth tax on billionaires), Proposition 40 is nullified, even if Proposition 40 also passes.

This proposition would make it harder to pass new special taxes by requiring the state auditor to review any special tax proposal before it goes to voters.
The auditor would assess whether the program that would receive funding could cut spending by at least 10% annually.
Any new special tax approved by voters would count toward California’s spending limit, potentially triggering automatic refunds that reduce funding for other state programs.
If this proposition receives more votes than Proposition 40 (a wealth tax on billionaires), Proposition 40 is nullified, even if Proposition 40 also passes.

This proposition would make it harder to pass new special taxes by requiring the state auditor to review any special tax proposal before it goes to voters.

If this proposition receives more votes than Proposition 40 (a wealth tax on billionaires), Proposition 40 is nullified, even if Proposition 40 also passes.

#### Proposition 41
##### Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues From State Spending Limit. Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes. Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
A **YES** vote on this measure means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot.
The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature.
In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
A **NO** vote on this measure means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change.
The state spending limit requirements would not change.

# Support dwindles for wealth tax, voter ID ballot measures, new poll shows
California voters are souring on a Nov. 3 ballot measure to impose a one-time tax on billionaires to help fund healthcare programs, a proposal that has triggered one of the most expensive political battles in state history.
Half of likely voters plan to vote against Proposition 40, the proposed wealth tax on billionaires’ assets, while 42% support it, according to a new poll by UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies that was co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times.
...
### Your guide to Proposition 40: California’s billionaire tax proposal
Nearly $368 million has been contributed to efforts opposing the billionaire tax, while $36 million has been donated to support the proposed levy.
...
The campaign against the wealth tax, funded by some of California’s richest tech moguls, is centered on three intertwined ballot initiatives: Proposition 40 and Propositions 41 and 42, both of which would undercut Proposition 40 through a series of changes to state tax laws and spending restrictions.
Proposition 41 would cut wasteful government spending by requiring audits of new state special taxes and would bar new state taxes that are exempt from a state spending limit.
Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on retirement holdings, individually owned assets and other personal savings.
Both Propositions 41 and 42 would nullify the billionaire tax if it passes, provided either measure receives more votes.

# Support slips for Prop 40 and Prop 45
The trendlines are troubling for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time wealth tax on California’s billionaires, and for Proposition 45, which would streamline environmental reviews for construction projects.
Support for both measures has slipped markedly in the last month, according to the Public Policy Institute of California, as ballots hit mailboxes and millions of dollars in negative ads inundated the airwaves.
The wealth tax has seen an especially big swing: Support fell from 52% in September to 46% this month, while opposition rose from 46% to 52% — the first time a prominent public poll has found a majority of voters opposing the measure.
But Prop 45 also plunged underwater.
Opposition leads 50-46, reversing the measure’s 49-46 advantage in PPIC’s September poll.
...

Half of likely voters plan to vote against Proposition 40, the proposed wealth tax on billionaires’ assets, while 42% support it, according to a new poll by UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies that was co-sponsored by the Los Angeles Times.

### Your guide to Proposition 40: California’s billionaire tax proposal

...
The campaign against the wealth tax, funded by some of California’s richest tech moguls, is centered on three intertwined ballot initiatives: Proposition 40 and Propositions 41 and 42, both of which would undercut Proposition 40 through a series of changes to state tax laws and spending restrictions.
Proposition 41 would cut wasteful government spending by requiring audits of new state special taxes and would bar new state taxes that are exempt from a state spending limit.
Proposition 42 would prohibit new taxes on retirement holdings, individually owned assets and other personal savings.
Both Propositions 41 and 42 would nullify the billionaire tax if it passes, provided either measure receives more votes.

# 2 new polls find Proposition 40 is on track to fail
California's billionaire tax could be headed toward defeat after two separate polls released this week found that Proposition 40 is losing support among voters.
...
The Public Policy Institute of California released a poll Tuesday evening that found Proposition 40 is on track to fail, with only 46% of voters saying they would vote in favor of the billionaire tax, meaning less than the majority needed to pass the measure are in favor.
Another poll from SurveyUSA also found that after leading by 8 points last month, it is now polling at only 44%, a lead of just one percentage point.
...
Opponents have also put their energy into Proposition 41 and Proposition 42, two other measures that contain language that could nullify Prop.
40 if they are passed.
PPIC's poll found Proposition 41, which would require audits of special state taxes and prevent any future ones, has 48% of likely voters in support and 49% of likely voters not in support.
The PPIC poll found that more Republican and moderate voters are in favor, with 81% of Republicans and 49% of moderates in support, compared with fewer Democrats, with just 28% supporting it.

PROP
41
PROHIBITS NEW STATE TAXES THAT EXCLUDE REVENUES FROM STATE SPENDING LIMIT. REQUIRES AUDITS FOR NEW STATE SPECIAL TAXES. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Nullifies state taxes enacted after January 1, 2026 that exempt their revenues from voter-approved state spending limit. Requires pre-election and recurring audits of programs funded by new special taxes. Fiscal Impact: The net fiscal effect is unknown as it depends on future decisions by voters, the Legislature, and other policymakers. Supporters: CA Society of Certified Public Accountants (CalCPAs); CalAsian Chamber of Commerce; California Taxpayers Association (CalTax) Opponents: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: When special taxes are proposed by voter initiatives, the California State Auditor would review programs funded by the tax before the initiative appears on the ballot. The California State Auditor also would regularly review programs funded by special taxes approved by voters or the Legislature. In addition, the state might not be able to exclude any new special tax spending from its spending limit.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The California State Auditor’s responsibility to review government programs would not change. The state spending limit requirements would not change.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Californians deserve better results for our taxes. Billions have flowed into programs like homelessness, with too little to show for it. Prop. 41 requires the independent State Auditor to conduct PUBLIC AUDITS of programs funded by new taxes—so we get more transparency, more accountability and better outcomes for taxpayers.
CON
Prop. 41 isn’t really about audits—it’s a billionaire-funded trick designed to undo the California Billionaire Tax. Billionaires would rather millions of Californians lose healthcare than pay a modest tax on their extreme wealth. Don’t fall for the billionaires’ lies. Vote NO on 41.

# Proposition 41
Prohibits New State Taxes That Exclude Revenues From State Spending Limit.
Requires Audits for New State Special Taxes.
Initiative Constitutional Amendment.
## Analysis of Measure
### Proposal
***Requires One-Time Audits Before Special Taxes Appear on the Ballot Through the Voter Initiative Process.*** Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to review each program that would receive funds from a new or increased special tax proposed through the voter initiative process.
This audit would occur after supporters collect 25 percent of the signatures needed to qualify a measure for the ballot, which is before it is known whether the initiative will qualify for the ballot.
Proposition 41 specifies what the State Auditor would include in these audits, including identifying ways to reduce an audited program’s annual costs by 10 percent.
Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor to write a summary of each audit.
If a proposed voter initiative with a special tax qualifies for the ballot, Proposition 41 requires the State Auditor’s summary to be included in the VIG*.* If voters approve the special tax, the cost of the one-time audit would be paid from the new tax revenues.

## Proposition 41: Restricts certain new state taxes and requires audits of special taxes
Proposition 41 would limit the state's ability to enact certain new taxes that exempt revenue from California's constitutional spending limit.
It would also require audits of new special tax proposals before they're placed on the ballot.
A yes vote would establish the proposed restrictions and auditing requirements.
A no vote would leave the existing rules in place.
Supporters say the measure would strengthen fiscal accountability and limit the state's ability to avoid constitutional spending restrictions.
Critics argue that the proposal could restrict future state revenue options and interfere with other tax measures, including the proposed billionaire wealth tax under Proposition 40.
If both Proposition 40 and Proposition 41 pass, Proposition 40 could be invalidated if Proposition 41 wins more votes.

## What does California Proposition 41 do?
This proposition would make it harder to pass new special taxes by requiring the state auditor to review any special tax proposal before it goes to voters.
The auditor would assess whether the program that would receive funding could cut spending by at least 10% annually.
Any new special tax approved by voters would count toward California’s spending limit, potentially triggering automatic refunds that reduce funding for other state programs.
If this proposition receives more votes than Proposition 40 (a wealth tax on billionaires), Proposition 40 is nullified, even if Proposition 40 also passes.
